To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the effects of deprivation upon responding in the initial link are more complex than previously thought, and that the S(r)-S(D) dissociation is not a necessary consequence of changes in deprivation level.

the discriminative and conditioned reinforcement functions of a stimulus can be weakened by satiation, and that the extent of this weakening is a function of deprivation level, maintenance on a satiation procedure, and the duration of maintenance.

the discriminative and conditioned-reinforcing functions of the stimulus associated with the final link in a two-link chained fixed-ratio schedule are affected differentially by satiation, but that these functions are equally affected by a change in deprivation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interaction of deprivation level and the strength of stimulus control in the two links of a chained schedule.
the dissociation of discriminant and conditioned reinforcement functions of stimuli.
the effects of satiety and deprivation upon the discriminative and reinforcing functions of stimuli.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the S(r)-S(D) dissociations observed in previous experiments may be due, in part, to the interaction of satiation and the maintenance procedure.
the S(r)-S(D) distinction has a basis in the behavior of the organism, but that the distinction is not as clear-cut as it was once thought to be.
the S(r), but not the S(D) functions are more readily weakened by changes in deprivation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the S(r), but not the S(D), function is disrupted by satiation.
the S(r)-S(D) distinction is a useful heuristic device but that the two functions are not independent.
the discriminative and reinforcing functions of stimuli are differentially affected by satiation and that these effects may be altered by the duration of maintenance in the satiation procedure.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the S(r), but not the S(D) functions of stimuli can be disrupted by satiation.

the S(r)-S(D) distinction may be a useful one to make in studies of behavior maintained by chained schedules, and that the S(r)/S(D) distinction can be used to study the effects of satiety and other physiological states on behavior.

, in a two-link chained fixed-ratio schedule, changes in deprivation level affect responding differentially in the two links, and that the effect is dependent upon the duration of maintenance of the satiation procedure.
